Assume Countable Choice. Fix $m\ge1$ and angles $0<\theta_j<\pi$ for $1\le j\le m$. On the strip $S=\mathbb R\times[0,1]$ impose the real product-plane boundary conditions $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$ and $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Let $H^1_\theta$ be the completion of smooth maps satisfying these conditions and compactly supported in the $s$ direction, for the norm
$$\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|u_s\|_2^2+\|u_t\|_2^2.$$
The real linear operator $D=\partial_s+i\partial_t$ extends to an isomorphism $H^1_\theta\to L^2(S;\mathbb C^m)$. Put $\gamma=\min_j\{\theta_j,\pi-\theta_j\}>0$. Its inverse satisfies
$$\|D^{-1}f\|_2\le\gamma^{-1}\|f\|_2,\qquad \|D^{-1}f\|_{H^1}\le\sqrt{\gamma^{-2}+5}\,\|f\|_2.$$
For $0\le\delta<\gamma$, set $w(s)=e^{\delta|s|}$, $H^1_{\theta,\delta}=\{u:wu\in H^1_\theta\}$ with norm $\|wu\|_{H^1}$, and $L^2_\delta=\{f:wf\in L^2\}$ with norm $\|wf\|_2$. Then $D:H^1_{\theta,\delta}\to L^2_\delta$ is an isomorphism and
$$\|D^{-1}f\|_{H^1_{\theta,\delta}}\le\frac{\sqrt{\gamma^{-2}+5}}{1-\delta/\gamma}\,\|f\|_{L^2_\delta},\qquad \|wD^{-1}f\|_2\le\frac{\|wf\|_2}{\gamma-\delta}.$$
These are estimates for the constant linear asymptotic model. They make no assertion about nonlinear strip decay, a variable-coefficient operator, or its Maslov index.

Assume Countable Choice. On $S=\mathbb R\times[0,1]$ use the real Hilbert domain $H^1_\theta$ with product-line boundary conditions at angles $0<\theta_j<\pi$: it is the $H^1$ completion of smooth maps compactly supported in the first coordinate and satisfying $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$, $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Let $B(s,t)$ be a bounded measurable real linear endomorphism of $\mathbb C^m$. Suppose there are real diagonal constant matrices $B_\pm=\operatorname{diag}(b_{\pm,1},\ldots,b_{\pm,m})$ such that
$$\underset{\pm s>R,\ 0<t<1}{\operatorname{ess\,sup}}\|B(s,t)-B_\pm\|\longrightarrow0\quad(R\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and $\theta_j-b_{\pm,j}\notin\pi\mathbb Z$ for every $j$ and each sign. Then
$$T=\partial_s+i\partial_t+B(s,t):H^1_\theta\longrightarrow L^2(S;\mathbb C^m)$$
is bounded and Fredholm over $\mathbb R$: its kernel and cokernel are finite dimensional and its range is closed. There are bounded left and right parametrices whose errors are operator-norm limits of finite-rank operators. No index value or identification with a Maslov index is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $m\ge1$ and $0<\theta_j<\pi$. Let $X=H^1_\theta$ be the real Hilbert completion, in the norm $(\|u\|_2^2+\|u_s\|_2^2+\|u_t\|_2^2)^{1/2}$, of smooth maps on $\mathbb R_s\times[0,1]_t$ compactly supported in $s$ and satisfying $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$, $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Put $Y=L^2(\mathbb R\times[0,1];\mathbb C^m)$, regarded as a real Hilbert space. Suppose $B(s,t)$ is an essentially bounded measurable real linear endomorphism and has real diagonal limits $B_\pm=\operatorname{diag}(b_{\pm,j})$ uniformly in essential supremum as $s\to\pm\infty$, with $\theta_j-b_{\pm,j}\notin\pi\mathbb Z$. Then the bounded Fredholm operator
$$T=\partial_s+i\partial_t+B:X\longrightarrow Y$$
has real index
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}T=\sum_{j=1}^m\left(\left\lfloor\frac{\theta_j-b_{-,j}}\pi\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{\theta_j-b_{+,j}}\pi\right\rfloor\right).$$
For the diagonal step function $B^0(s)=B_-$ for $s<0$ and $B_+$ for $s\ge0$, the kernel has one real generator for every $(j,n)\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\times\mathbb Z$ with $\lambda_{-,j,n}<0<\lambda_{+,j,n}$, and the cokernel has one for every pair with $\lambda_{-,j,n}>0>\lambda_{+,j,n}$, where $\lambda_{\pm,j,n}=\pi n-\theta_j+b_{\pm,j}$.

The same index holds on the two-sided weighted spaces $X_\delta=\{u:e^{\delta|s|}u\in X\}$ and $Y_\delta=\{f:e^{\delta|s|}f\in Y\}$ whenever $0\le\delta<\min_{j,\pm,n}|\lambda_{\pm,j,n}|$. This is an index theorem for this specified strip operator and product-line domain; it does not identify the pullback operator of a general geometric strip or assert a Heegaard-domain Maslov formula.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a smooth real rank-$2m$ vector bundle on $S=\mathbb R_s\times[0,1]_t$, $m\ge1$, with a smooth endomorphism $J$ satisfying $J^2=-I$. On the two boundary edges let $F_0,F_1$ be smooth real rank-$m$ subbundles with $F_j\cap JF_j=0$. Suppose that outside a compact strip there are specified smooth complex frames $\tau_\pm:\mathbb C^m\to E$, intertwining $i$ and $J$, in which $F_0=\mathbb R^m$ and $F_1=i\mathbb R^m$. Let $P$ be a smooth real linear first-order operator on sections of $E$ with symbol
$$P(f\xi)=fP\xi+f_s\xi+f_tJ\xi$$
for every smooth real function $f$, and suppose its expression in each end frame is exactly $\partial_s+i\partial_t$ outside a compact strip.

There exist a global smooth complex frame $\Phi$, a sign matrix $S_+=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,1,\ldots,1)$ with $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$, an integer $\ell$, and a smooth real function $\vartheta(s)$, constant at $\pi/2$ on the negative end and $\pi/2+\ell\pi$ on the positive end, such that $\Phi=\tau_-$ on the negative end, $\Phi=\tau_+S_+$ on the positive end, and
$$F_0=\Phi\mathbb R^m,\qquad F_1=\Phi\left(e^{i\vartheta(s)}\mathbb R\times i\mathbb R^{m-1}\right).$$
In this frame $P$ is $\partial_s+i\partial_t+B(s,t)$ with smooth compactly supported real linear $B$. On the $H^1$ completion of compactly supported smooth sections satisfying those actual boundary subbundles, with the norm defined by finite bundle charts on a compact core and the prescribed frames on the ends, $P$ maps to the corresponding $L^2(E)$ space and is real Fredholm, with
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}P=-\ell.$$
The same index holds with the weight $e^{\delta|s|}$ for $0\le\delta<\pi/2$. These are indices before any translation quotient. The integer $\ell$ is independent of the choices in the construction, since it is minus the index of this fixed operator.

In particular the conclusion applies to the actual linearization at a smooth $J_t$-holomorphic strip of finite Dirichlet energy, measured in a smooth target metric, in a compact target, with compact totally real boundary submanifolds of transverse finite intersection, whenever the chosen target charts at their intersections identify those submanifolds with $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$ and $J_t$ with the constant structure $i$ for every $t$. For product Heegaard tori such a geometric choice is available by the product-integrable generator-neighborhood construction. No domain Euler-measure formula, corner/excision theorem, generic regularity, or moduli count is part of this conclusion.

derivations.claim: **Weak derivatives from bounded tests.** We first record the precise Hilbert argument used below. If a distribution $v$ is in $L^2$ and $|\int v\,\partial_j\phi|\le M\|\phi\|_2$ for all smooth compact interior tests, this functional extends uniquely to the closure of that test space in $L^2$, which is all of $L^2$. The density assertion follows by cutting off in $s$, removing boundary strips of width tending to zero, and convolving on the resulting interior rectangles; convergence is first checked for step functions and then in $L^2$. By the orthogonal projection construction in [F2], every bounded real functional $L$ on a Hilbert space has a representing vector: if $L\ne0$, take $z$ with $L(z)\ne0$, put $z_\perp=z-\operatorname{proj}_{\ker L}z$, and write $x-(L(x)/L(z_\perp))z_\perp\in\ker L$. This gives $L(x)=L(z_\perp)\langle x,z_\perp\rangle/\|z_\perp\|^2$; the zero functional is represented by zero. Hence $v$ has weak derivative in $L^2$ of norm at most $M$. In particular, if $v_h\to v$ in $L^2$ and $\|v_h\|_{H^1}\le M$, then $v\in H^1$ with the corresponding bounds. Integration against interior tests proves each derivative assertion; approximating any $L^2$ test by smooth ones proves weak convergence of the derivatives, and therefore weak $H^1$ convergence. A closed Hilbert subspace is weakly closed, since pairing with its orthogonal complement vanishes and the orthogonal projection decomposition is exhaustive. These arguments use only the Countable-Choice projections of [F2].

**A tangential difference quotient keeps exactly the permitted boundary condition.** For $u\in X_0$ and $h\ne0$ set $\delta_hu(s,t)=(u(s+h,t)-u(s,t))/h$. Translation and subtraction preserve $X_0$, first on its defining smooth maps and then by completion. The fundamental theorem of calculus in $s$, followed by Cauchy–Schwarz and integration, gives $\|\delta_hu\|_2\le\|u_s\|_2$. It also proves $\delta_hu\to u_s$ strongly in $L^2$ by approximation in $H^1$ by the defining smooth maps. The same argument gives $\|\delta_hf\|_2\le\|f_s\|_2$ for $f\in H^1$, by interior approximation and the usual one-dimensional slicing identity, which itself follows by integrating the weak derivative against product tests. If $T_0u=f\in H^1$, put $B_h(s,t)=B(s+h,t)$. The weak product rule, obtained by testing and smooth approximation, gives $D\delta_hu=\delta_hf-B_h\delta_hu-(\delta_h B)u$. Since $\|\delta_hB\|_\infty\le\|B_s\|_\infty$, [F1] yields $\|\delta_hu\|_{H^1}\le C(\|f_s\|_2+\|B\|_\infty\|u_s\|_2+\|B_s\|_\infty\|u\|_2)$ uniformly for $h\ne0$. By step 1.1, $u_s\in H^1$ with this bound. It belongs to $X_0$ by weak closedness, because every difference quotient does. This is why no differentiated normal boundary condition has been imposed.

**Recover the normal derivatives and iterate.** The equation gives $u_t=-i(f-Bu-u_s)$. For $f\in H^1$ the right side is in $H^1$ by step 2.1 and the bounded first derivatives of $B$. Thus both $u_s,u_t\in H^1$, giving $u\in H^2$ and the claimed estimate for $q=1$. For the induction suppose the conclusion is known for order $q-1\ge1$ and $f\in H^q$. The already proved lower orders give $u\in H^q$ and $u_s\in X_0$. Differentiating distributionally gives $T_0u_s=f_s-B_su\in H^{q-1}$. Apply the order-$q-1$ result to this equation, to get $u_s\in H^q$ with its bound. The formula for $u_t$ then gives $u_t\in H^q$. All weak derivatives of order at most $q+1$ are therefore in $L^2$. The Leibniz rule and the finitely many bounded derivatives of $B$ give $\|u\|_{H^{q+1}}\le C_q(\|f\|_{H^q}+\|u\|_{H^1})$ by the induction bounds. The case $q=0$ is immediate. The argument has differentiated only in the tangential direction before using the equation to recover normal derivatives.

**Identify range and cokernel, not just nullspaces.** The space $X_q$ is a closed real subspace of $H^{q+1}$: convergence there implies convergence in $H^1$, where $X_0$ is closed by [F1]. It is Hilbert, and the bounded derivatives of $B$ make $T_q$ bounded. Step 3.1 with $f=0$ proves $\ker T_q=\ker T_0$. The same step for arbitrary $f\in Y_q$ proves $\operatorname{Ran}T_q=Y_q\cap\operatorname{Ran}T_0$. This range is closed in $Y_q$ because $\operatorname{Ran}T_0$ is closed in $L^2$ by [F2]. The quotient map $Y_q\to L^2/\operatorname{Ran}T_0$ is surjective: smooth compactly supported interior functions are dense in $L^2$ by the explicit approximation in step 1.1 and belong to $Y_q$, so its image is dense; the image is a linear subspace of a finite-dimensional space and hence closed, as follows by choosing a basis and the finite-dimensional Euclidean lower norm bound. Its kernel is precisely $\operatorname{Ran}T_q$. This proves the asserted cokernel isomorphism and Fredholmness. Both kernel and cokernel dimensions agree with $q=0$, and [F3] gives the displayed index.

**Smooth weights.** Put $v=wu$. Direct differentiation gives $wT_0w^{-1}v=Dv+(B-\delta\rho')v$. This new coefficient has all derivatives bounded and real diagonal limits $b_{-,j}+\delta$ and $b_{+,j}-\delta$. The spectral-gap bound ensures that no limiting eigenvalue crosses zero when $\delta$ is increased from zero to its stated value; hence the endpoint floors in [F3] stay constant. Apply steps 2.1–4.1 to this conjugated operator. Multiplication by $w$ is an isometric identification by the definitions of the weighted spaces and preserves their real-line boundary conditions. Thus it transfers all kernel, range, cokernel and regularity assertions, as well as the index. Smoothness of $\rho$ at zero is essential for this high-order argument. At order one these spaces agree with those defined using $e^{\delta|s|}$ up to equivalent norms, since the ratio and its reciprocal are bounded Lipschitz functions constant outside a compact interval.

**Transfer to the actual geometric operator.** In [F4] the frame matrices on a finite compact core are smooth, and their comparisons on the two ends are constant; every derivative is bounded. The extra scalar/product gauge $U$ has all derivatives bounded because its angle is smooth and constant outside a compact interval, while $0\le t\le1$. Its inverse has the same property. The repeated Leibniz rule therefore makes frame and gauge multiplication bounded isomorphisms on each of the finitely charted geometric $H^r$ spaces for every integer $r\ge0$. They identify precisely the zeroth boundary trace, without restricting any higher derivative. After these transformations the actual operator has fixed product-line domain and a smooth zeroth-order coefficient with all derivatives bounded and real diagonal end limits; the scalar gauge contributes $-a+i a't$, whose limits are real. Thus steps 3.1–5.1 apply to the actual $H^{q+1}\to H^q$ operator, including the smooth weighted realizations. The transformations commute with scalar weights. The resulting common real index is the actual $H^1$ index supplied by [F4], and nothing has been subtracted for translations.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $G:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb C)$ be smooth. Its determinant winding is the integer
$$w(G)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_0^1\frac{(\det G)'(s)}{\det G(s)}\,ds.$$
There is a smooth map $\widehat G:\overline{\mathbb D}\to\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb C)$ restricting to $G$ on the positively oriented boundary if and only if $w(G)=0$. When it exists the extension can be chosen independent of radius on a boundary collar. More generally a prescribed smooth invertible matrix map on a collar of the disk boundary extends smoothly to the disk, agreeing on a smaller boundary collar, exactly when its boundary determinant winding is zero. The construction is finite dimensional and choice-free.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a smooth real rank-$2m$ vector bundle on $S=\mathbb R_s\times[0,1]_t$, $m\ge1$, with a smooth endomorphism $J$ satisfying $J^2=-I$. On the two boundary edges let $F_0,F_1$ be smooth real rank-$m$ subbundles with $F_j\cap JF_j=0$. Suppose that outside a compact strip there are specified smooth complex frames $\tau_\pm:\mathbb C^m\to E$, intertwining $i$ and $J$, in which $F_0=\mathbb R^m$ and $F_1=i\mathbb R^m$. Let $P$ be a smooth real linear first-order operator on sections of $E$ with symbol
$$P(f\xi)=fP\xi+f_s\xi+f_tJ\xi$$
for every smooth real function $f$, and suppose its expression in each end frame is exactly $\partial_s+i\partial_t$ outside a compact strip.

There exist a global smooth complex frame $\Phi$, a sign matrix $S_+=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,1,\ldots,1)$ with $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$, an integer $\ell$, and a smooth real function $\vartheta(s)$, constant at $\pi/2$ on the negative end and $\pi/2+\ell\pi$ on the positive end, such that $\Phi=\tau_-$ on the negative end, $\Phi=\tau_+S_+$ on the positive end, and
$$F_0=\Phi\mathbb R^m,\qquad F_1=\Phi\left(e^{i\vartheta(s)}\mathbb R\times i\mathbb R^{m-1}\right).$$
In this frame $P$ is $\partial_s+i\partial_t+B(s,t)$ with smooth compactly supported real linear $B$. On the $H^1$ completion of compactly supported smooth sections satisfying those actual boundary subbundles, with the norm defined by finite bundle charts on a compact core and the prescribed frames on the ends, $P$ maps to the corresponding $L^2(E)$ space and is real Fredholm, with
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}P=-\ell.$$
The same index holds with the weight $e^{\delta|s|}$ for $0\le\delta<\pi/2$. These are indices before any translation quotient. The integer $\ell$ is independent of the choices in the construction, since it is minus the index of this fixed operator.

In particular the conclusion applies to the actual linearization at a smooth $J_t$-holomorphic strip of finite Dirichlet energy, measured in a smooth target metric, in a compact target, with compact totally real boundary submanifolds of transverse finite intersection, whenever the chosen target charts at their intersections identify those submanifolds with $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$ and $J_t$ with the constant structure $i$ for every $t$. For product Heegaard tori such a geometric choice is available by the product-integrable generator-neighborhood construction. No domain Euler-measure formula, corner/excision theorem, generic regularity, or moduli count is part of this conclusion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $S=\mathbb R_s\times[0,1]_t$, $m\ge1$, and $0<\theta_j<\pi$. Write $X_0=H^1_\theta$ for the real $H^1$ completion of smooth maps compactly supported in $s$ satisfying $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$ and $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Let $B:S\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb R}(\mathbb C^m)$ be smooth up to the boundary, with every derivative bounded, and suppose its uniform end limits are real diagonal matrices $\operatorname{diag}(b_{\pm,j})$ with $\theta_j-b_{\pm,j}\notin\pi\mathbb Z$. For an integer $q\ge0$ put
$$X_q=H^{q+1}(S;\mathbb C^m)\cap X_0,\qquad Y_q=H^q(S;\mathbb C^m),\qquad T_q=\partial_s+i\partial_t+B:X_q\longrightarrow Y_q,$$
using real Hilbert spaces and their indicated Sobolev norms. There are no higher boundary conditions: only the zeroth trace encoded by $X_0$ is required. In particular no normal derivative or forcing trace is prescribed.

Every $T_q$ is bounded Fredholm. Its kernel is the same set as the kernel of $T_0$, and its range is $Y_q\cap\operatorname{Ran}T_0$. The inclusion of $Y_q$ in $L^2$ induces an isomorphism of real cokernels. Thus
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}T_q=\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}T_0=\sum_j\left(\left\lfloor\frac{\theta_j-b_{-,j}}\pi\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{\theta_j-b_{+,j}}\pi\right\rfloor\right).$$
More precisely, if $u\in X_0$ and $T_0u=f\in H^q$, then $u\in X_q$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{q+1}}\le C_q\bigl(\|f\|_{H^q}+\|u\|_{H^1}\bigr).$$

The same conclusions hold with smooth two-sided weights $w=e^{\delta\rho(s)}$, where $\rho$ is smooth, equals $|s|$ outside a compact interval, has all derivatives of positive order bounded, and $0\le\delta<\min_{\pm,j,n}|\pi n-\theta_j+b_{\pm,j}|$. Weighted spaces mean $wu\in X_q$ and $wf\in Y_q$. Their index is the same displayed index. The weight is smooth at zero even for $q\ge1$.

Finally, for an actual geometric strip operator with exact product-integrable ends and the smooth bundle frame supplied by the geometric strip normal-form theorem, the actual $H^{q+1}$ boundary-section domain and $H^q$ target have this same real index before translation quotient, also with these smooth weights. This asserts integer Hilbert Sobolev agreement; no $W^{1,p}$ comparison or Heegaard-domain Euler formula is asserted.

derivations.claim: **Squared phase is well defined, including unoriented boundary bundles.** A real basis of a totally real $m$-plane in $\mathbb C^m$ is complex independent: a complex dependence would express a vector in the plane also in its $i$ multiple, and splitting the dependence into real and imaginary parts forces both to vanish. A real basis change multiplies its complex determinant by a nonzero real determinant; its squared normalized phase is therefore unchanged. Local frames give one continuous map $\zeta$ even when a global oriented real basis does not exist. For a continuous loop into $S^1$, subdivide its parameter interval into finitely many subintervals whose images lie in open arcs of length less than $2\pi$. Each arc has an explicit continuous argument, for instance by the local arctangent after a fixed rotation. Add integer multiples of $2\pi$ successively so that neighboring arguments agree. The final argument differs from the initial one by $2\pi$ times an integer; this is winding. Refinement does not change that integer, so neither does the initial subdivision. Products add their argument changes. A homotopy of loops preserves this integer: uniform continuity permits a finite subdivision in both parameters with all relevant pointwise ratios in an arc about one, so adjacent loops have continuously chosen ratio argument with zero endpoint difference. This proves homotopy invariance by finitely many comparisons.

**Frame invariance and the actual index sign.** A change of global complex frame on $Q$ multiplies $\zeta$ by the normalized square of an inverse complex determinant of a matrix defined on all of $Q$. Its boundary determinant has winding zero by [F1], so $M$ is unchanged. Work now in the actual frame $\Phi$ of [F2]. On the bottom $\zeta=1$. On the top it is $e^{2i\vartheta(s)}(-1)^{m-1}$. The right end cap has squared phase change $m\pi$ as $t$ increases from zero to one; the real factor $S_+^{-1}$ has squared normalized determinant one. The left end cap, traversed downwards, has change $-m\pi$. The top is traversed from positive to negative $s$, with phase change $-2\ell\pi$, while the bottom is constant. Total phase change is thus $-2\ell\pi$, giving $M=-\ell=\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}P$. Near each corner $\rho$ is constant and the horizontal boundary planes are constant in their end frame, so this boundary loop is smooth after rounding the parameter corners and has the computed winding. Altering $\rho$ gives a homotopy fixing its endpoint planes; enlarging $Q$ only inserts constant horizontal portions and identical product caps in the exact end frame. Step 1.1 proves the claimed independence. Finally [F3] gives the stated equality on all the higher Sobolev and weighted realizations; the end gap is $\pi/2$.

**Finite planar excision.** Let $K$ be the punctured rectangle in the Statement. Squared phase of the subbundle defines a continuous map $\zeta:K\to S^1$ by step 1.1. Uniform continuity gives a positive mesh size such that the image of $K$ intersected with any square of smaller diameter lies in one proper open arc of $S^1$; choose a point of this nonempty intersection and use a rotated arctangent on the arc about its image. Lay down finitely many horizontal and vertical lines at this mesh size. Shift them slightly, if necessary, to avoid tangencies to the finitely many hole circles and their topmost, bottommost, leftmost and rightmost points; each line has only finitely many excluded values. Choose the vertical lines first, then choose the horizontal ones also avoiding the finitely many heights of circle intersections with vertical lines, so no grid vertex lies on a hole circle. Their intersections with the circles and the outer rectangle are finite. Each cell intersected with $K$ is a finite planar region bounded by finitely many straight segments and circle arcs. Its boundary can be traversed as finitely many closed cycles by following those arcs and segments, with the region on the left; this is a finite graph operation, using the two incident edges at an ordinary boundary vertex and keeping separate the cycles of disconnected components. Every such cycle lies in a single square where $\zeta$ has a continuous real argument. Hence its total argument change is zero by telescoping endpoint differences over its segments. Add over the finitely many cells. On internal square segments the opposite traversals have opposite changes; the change is independent of the selected local argument because any two lifts along a segment differ by a constant multiple of $2\pi$. Only the outer boundary and clockwise hole circles remain. Thus outer winding minus the sum of counterclockwise hole windings is zero. Smoothness is unnecessary for this identity. In a smooth model its winding may equivalently be obtained by integrating the derivative of a local argument, since the one-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus gives the same endpoint differences.

**A source-cover branch.** For the displayed double cover the vectors $v$ on the two source sheets are sent by $dq$ to $(v,\sqrt w\,v)$ and $(v,-\sqrt w\,v)$, in the ordering $z_1=-\sqrt w,z_2=\sqrt w$. Their determinant is $-2\sqrt w\,v^2$. It never vanishes on the circle, and its square is $4w v^4$, whose phase winds once. The sheet ordering interchanges after a full circuit but this changes determinant by a real sign only, leaving the squared phase unchanged. More generally write the roots as $z_j=\omega^j a$, $a^r=w$, $\omega=e^{2\pi i/r}$. The derivative of the elementary symmetric coordinate map has determinant, up to a fixed nonzero sign, $\prod_{j<k}(z_j-z_k)$. To verify that identity, its determinant is an alternating polynomial in the $z_j$ because exchanging variables exchanges columns. It is divisible by each $z_j-z_k$, has their total degree $r(r-1)/2$, and is not the zero polynomial: at distinct roots, a variation leaving all elementary symmetric coefficients fixed would give the zero polynomial $\sum_j\delta z_j\prod_{k\ne j}(t-z_k)$; evaluation at $t=z_j$ forces every $\delta z_j=0$. Thus the determinant is a nonzero constant times that product. Sending each source vector to the same $v$ multiplies determinant by $v^r$. Its square is a nonzero constant times $a^{r(r-1)}=w^{r-1}$. The squared phase consequently winds $r-1$, also for $r=1$, when the empty product is one. Distinct additional sheets separated from this cluster introduce nonzero factors extending across the small disk and hence winding zero; in the stated fixed-product version they simply multiply by a nonzero constant.

**Target ramification and source vector zeros.** On an unbranched parameter sheet with source coordinate $z$, the derivative of $f(z)=z^{r+1}$ sends $v$ to $(r+1)z^r v$. The square of its normalized phase has argument change twice that of $z^r$, namely $4\pi r$ along a positive circle; its winding is $2r$. If instead a scalar source vector $v(z)$ is merely nonzero along the circle and winds $k$, multiplication of an otherwise nonsingular sheet direction by it multiplies the determinant phase by $v/|v|$, and its square contributes $2k$. The nonsingular factor has zero winding when it extends nonvanishing over the disk, by the argument-lift homotopy of step 1.1. A constant extra product basis contributes a constant nonzero determinant factor and does not alter winding.

**Direct sum and actual strip gluing.** In a direct-sum frame the determinant of concatenated bases is the product of the two determinants. Their squared phases multiply, so step 1.1 proves additivity of $M$. For gluing at matching ends, truncate in their exact constant regions and identify the end fibers by the matching product frames. The complex bundles and operators glue smoothly because all coefficients there have the same exact constant expressions; their horizontal totally real boundary data match. The glued bundle has a global complex frame by [F2], and its restriction is a global frame for each of the two cut rectangles. The squared phase along the inserted shared cap is identical for the two rectangles and traversed in opposite directions. All its argument changes cancel. The remaining changes are precisely those on the boundary loop of the glued problem, so its $M$ is the sum of the two separate $M$ values. Frame invariance from step 2.1 allows the restricted global frame in this computation instead of the individual normal-form frames. Applying step 2.1 to all three actual operators proves index additivity. No assertion about gluing nonlinear solutions has been used.

**A transverse graph node, with its oriented sign.** In the graph model the two target points are $Az,Bz$. The chosen source directions map to $v,v$ respectively. In symmetric target coordinates the two columns are therefore $(v,(Bz)v)$ and $(v,(Az)v)$, and their determinant is $v^2(A-B)z$. The real invertible map $A-B$ sends a positive circle to an ellipse traversed with degree $\operatorname{sign}\det_{\mathbb R}(A-B)$. One direct verification uses real Gram–Schmidt to deform a positive determinant matrix through invertibles to a positive diagonal matrix and then to the identity; a negative determinant matrix is reduced in the same way to a reflection.
